before.problem:
$$
x={R}^{-1}\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
before.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,\bbox[6px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{|}{Q}^{T}\,\,}\,\,\bbox[6px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{|}b\phantom{|}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${Q}^{T}$ and $b.$

x=\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
before.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & =\bbox[6px,border: 1px solid black]{\,\phantom{|}\,\,{R}^{-1}\,}\,{Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are ${R}^{-1}$ and ${Q}^{T}.$

$$
R\,\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}=\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
after.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{|}x\phantom{|}} & ={Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $x$ and ${Q}^{T}.$

before.problem:
$$
\bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{x} = \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{b}

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
before.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, it satisfies $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

$$
R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\,R\phantom{|}}\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $Q^T.$

before.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

after.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

before.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}+x-2,$ then ${A}^{4}=$
before.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{4}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}+x-2,$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $+$ $3$
${x}^{2}+x-2\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{4}\phantom{|}\,\,\,}$
${x}^{4}$ $+$ ${x}^{3}$ $-$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ ${x}^{3}$ $+$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ ${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $+$ $2x$
$3{x}^{2}$ $-$ $2x$
$3{x}^{2}$ $+$ $3x$ $-$ $6$
$-$ $5x$ $+$ $6$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{4}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{4} & =q(x)p(x)+(-5x+6),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{2}-x+3.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{4}=q(A)p(A)+(-5A+6I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & =q(A)p(A)+(-5A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-5A+6I) \\ & =-5A+6I.\end{aligned} $$

before.worked_solution:

$\,\,x$ $+$ $1$
${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\phantom{|}\,\,}$
${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $-$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $+$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $-$ $20$
$21x$ $+$ $20$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)=x+1.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\ & =21A+20I.\end{aligned} $$
